title: Short codes for common letters
hook: 8 letters, 2 bits each, 16 bits. Can uneven codes do better?

doesNotKnow: that codes can have different lengths and still be decoded

misconception: Every symbol needs the same number of bits, so 8 symbols from 4 kinds always cost 16 bits.
objective: The learner can explain that each join adds one bit to every symbol beneath it, so joining the two rarest groups first gives common symbols short codes and rare ones long codes, and the message 4A 2B 1C 1D needs 14 bits instead of 16.

claims.text: Joining C + D, then that with B, then with A gives code lengths A 1, B 2, C 3, D 3, for 4x1 + 2x2 + 1x3 + 1x3 = 14 bits.
claims.source: Each symbol's code length is its depth in the tree. Equivalently each join adds its weight: 2 + 4 + 8 = 14. Builder computed both in Node.

claims.text: Fixed 2-bit codes for 8 symbols cost 16 bits.
Joining two groups adds one bit to the code of every symbol inside them, so a join costs its total weight in bits.
claims.source: A join makes the two groups children of a new node, lengthening every code beneath by one bit (0 for one side, 1 for the other). Total bits = sum over symbols of weight x depth = sum over joins of the joined weight.

claims.text: In a code read off such a tree, no code is the start of another, so a message can be decoded without separators.
claims.source: Codes are the paths to leaves; a leaf has no descendants, so no codeword is a prefix of another (prefix code). CLRS 3rd ed., 16.3 'Huffman codes'. Example from the brief's tree: 1, 01, 000, 001.

claims.text: Always joining the two lightest groups gives the fewest bits possible for any prefix code (Huffman coding).
claims.source: Huffman, 'A Method for the Construction of Minimum-Redundancy Codes', Proc. IRE 40(9), 1952; optimality proof in CLRS 3rd ed., 16.3, Lemmas 16.2-16.3 and Theorem 16.4.

claims.text: With two groups left, only one join is possible, so the stage makes it automatically.
claims.source: Demo.tsx join(): when the forest has two trees they are joined; any order gives the same total because the last join always costs the full weight (8).

claims.text: The tree you build by joining C + D, then B, then A gives the codes A 1, B 01, C 000, D 001.
claims.source: Demo.tsx joins (C,D), then (CD,B), then (CDB,A), labelling the left child 0 and the right 1: A is the right child of the root (1), B the right child of the left subtree (01), C and D are 000 and 001. Lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 match c1.

recall.question: Building a Huffman code, which two groups do you join first?
options: Any two neighbours in the alphabet
recall.why: Every join adds a bit to each symbol beneath it. Joining the rarest first puts the extra bits where they are used least, leaving common symbols with short codes.
